rv.q: “KPOP,” the musical, understands that, bringing to Broadway a rousing portrait of the minutiae of the industry, from its personal struggles and vexing complexities to its infectious musicality.
It's now the subject of an ambitious new immersive, interactive musical that is often as physically exhausting as it is wildly entertaining.
Fortunately, the music revives this dying party.
How sweet or inspiring is it, though, when we know that the thirteen-year-olds aren’t allowed to eat cake?
For them, the musical is less an eye-opener than an ear-pounder, assiduously drowning out any ambitions it may once have had to be more.
It feels as if the show has rushed out into the open water of Broadway and then gotten stuck, like a ship unable to catch the wind.
It is also, unfortunately, a lesson of KPOP itself, which has now arrived at Broadway's Circle in the Square with so much plastic surgery that it is barely recognizable.
The musical captures the slick professionalism and manufactured glamour of the K-pop industry, but struggles to find its own authentic voice beneath the glossy surface.
The musical's book, by Jason Kim, offers a behind-the-scenes look at the pressures and artifice of the K-pop industry, but the storytelling feels as manufactured as the pop confections it depicts.
KPOP The Musical is the most exciting, interesting, and alive show on Broadway right now.
See the show, and you’ll understand why K-pop and its stars have taken over the musical universe.

What makes “KPOP” transcend buoyant entertainment is its focus on the tensions underlying the exhilarating, dazzlingly precise song-and-dance routines on display here, courtesy of composer/lyricists Helen Park and Max Vernon and choreographer Jennifer Weber.
KPOP's stellar musical numbers and all-star cast are able to turn the beat around into a solid, feel-good joyride that both K-Pop and musical fans can appreciate.
On the other hand, KPOP, written by Jason Kim and directed by Teddy Bergman, has scarcely enough compelling substance to sustain its own first act.
All of this spells doom for KPOP, a delightful musical entertainment that is best appreciated as just that, and nothing more.
Under Teddy Bergman's direction, the show is in constant motion and the performers make use of the entire theatre, but the book scenes are flat and uninvolving.
But when the company sings the final song, "Blast Off," you may realize that you're having too much fun to notice–or care.
The production numbers bring the house down, but there’s not much else there.
Like the genre it celebrates, “KPOP” works best when you let yourself get caught up in the sensation of the music and the precision dance moves — and try not to think too deeply.
Well, you might be better off at home.
In contrast, its attempt at drama feels like meager filler, and unconvincingly glued on to the more music-y musical the production seems to be straining to be.
Which begs the question: with so many actual K-pop acts now appearing in the area on a regular basis, why not go for the real thing instead of a highly proficient reproduction?
But, in its journey to Midtown, a reimagined KPOP has abandoned its weightier self-awareness, along with a lot of its creativity.
I cannot think of a show that, in its commercial transfer, has managed so thoroughly to shed so much of its stardust.
If this is the future of Broadway, please consider me a rabid and reinvigorated stan.

tn.cat: Best Costume Design of a Musical
Best Costume Design of a Musical

cn.t: Critics find KPOP visually spectacular with electrifying performances and choreography, but the thin plot and weak storytelling undermine the dazzling production values, resulting in mostly mixed reviews.

sg.ra: In the 3/4 thrust configuration these front rows put you at the lip of the playing area with actors entering from aisles directly beside you. Headout notes rows AA-B are 'closest to the stage' and audiences are 'roped into the play's action.' Because the stage is surrounded on three sides, the acting is deliberately blocked so no front row gets a sustained back-of-actor view, but individual moments will face away from you — that is inherent to in-the-round and not a flaw of this section.

Universally cited as the optimal vantage in this thrust venue — close enough to feel the intimacy of a 776-seat room with only 10 rows, but one row back from the front so sightlines catch the whole three-sided playing area. Headout: 'Center Orchestra - rows B, C and D' positioned centrally are 'possibly the best seats in the house.' The in-the-round blocking is designed so these central rows at eye-level with the floor see choreography and staging as intended.

Because the venue only has 10 rows total and stadium-inclined seating, rows H-I still feel close to the thrust while giving elevated sightlines that reveal staging patterns on the floor — useful for musicals with choreography. Headout: 'Rows H and I in the upper middle level offer a great view of the stage and the prices are lower than those of the premium orchestra seats.' AVFMS reviewer MusicaltheatreWhiz in H144 (Just in Time, Feb 2026): 'There really isn't a bad seat in the house!' TripAdvisor: 'up is better for musicals.'

In a typical Broadway house the last row would be a skip, but Circle in the Square is only 10 rows deep so row K is roughly where Row G would be in a standard theater. AVFMS danielb9 at K109 (Just in Time, Feb 28 2026): 'Enough legroom to be comfortable and despite being in the back row felt very connected to the action.' Multiple reviews note 'no obstruction' and 'great seat' for row K. Stadium incline ensures sightlines over heads. The in-the-round nature means some scenes still play toward the opposite side, but this is a venue property not a section flaw.

sg.n: Side Sections - Long Arms of the Horseshoe (100s & 200s)
sg.ra: The two long 'wide sides' of the horseshoe (the 100 and 200 numbered sections per BWW forum user Patash's question about 102/202 numbering) give a profile view of the main action. TripAdvisor: 'the two wide sides are fine' and are preferred over 'straight in front' which is 'too far from the rear end of the main stage.' AVFMS samr32 at C207 (Just in Time, Feb 26 2026): 'Amazing seat! Can see both stages so well, and the actors (including Jonathan Groff) run up and down the aisle right near you.' The 300-degree blocking means side sections regularly get face-forward moments; not behind-stage.

The one sustained warning across every source is the extreme corner seats where the horseshoe's ends meet the stage. Headout/TickPick specifically: 'seats 438-440 are obstructed when actors perform on the far left of the stage and vice versa for the opposite side' (437-439). Unlike the rest of the house where in-the-round angles are temporary, these corner positions can have whole extended scenes played entirely out of view on the opposite corner. In a 3/4 thrust with actors using the full perimeter, this is a structural flaw of the seat, not a temporary blocking issue.
